Spark without the JVM

spark-without-the-jvm.Rmd

SparkR and sparklyr reach Spark through a local Spark installation and its JVM; pysparklyr reaches Spark Connect through Python. zuspark needs none of them. Spark Connect is gRPC carrying protocol buffers, with results as Arrow record batches, and each of those has an R implementation:

  • gRPC through zugrpc, on zuhttp’s HTTP/2 and the operating system’s TLS.
  • Protocol buffers through zuproto, which reads Spark’s message definitions at run time from a compiled descriptor set that zuspark ships, pinned to one Spark release.
  • Arrow through zuarrow, which decodes the batches and converts them to R, refusing a value R cannot hold exactly unless you say otherwise.

zuspark itself is R code over these packages: it has no compiled code of its own. zuspark_info() shows what it was built with.

library(zuspark)
zuspark_info()
#> zuspark 0.1.0, Spark Connect protocol v4.2.1
#>   descriptors: fba77546a88f7e96
#>   zuproto:     0.1.0
#>   zugrpc:      0.0.0.9000 on zuhttp 0.1.0

What a query costs

A query is two round trips. spark_sql() sends the statement and gets back the server’s plan for it, unexecuted; spark_collect() or spark_fetch() executes that plan and reads the result as it streams. The server keeps the result buffered until the client says it is done with it, so that a stream cut by a proxy or a timeout can be reattached where it stopped. zuspark releases what it has read as it goes, and the rest when the query finishes or fails.

con <- spark_connect()
q <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT id, id % 7 AS weekday, rand(42) AS amount FROM range(1000000)")
system.time(df <- spark_collect(q))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.204   0.041   0.709
nrow(df)
#> [1] 1000000
q
#> <zuspark_query> SELECT id, id % 7 AS weekday, rand(42) AS amount FROM range(1000000)
#>   on sc://127.0.0.1:15002 (last run: 1e+06 rows)

A Spark result in DuckDB

spark_fetch() returns the result as an Arrow stream rather than a data frame. Code that consumes Arrow can take it from there without the rows becoming R vectors first. DuckDB is one such consumer: here a summary is computed by Spark, and joined in DuckDB with a table that only exists locally.

DuckDB’s R package registers Arrow data through the arrow package, so the stream is converted to an arrow RecordBatchReader first. Loading nanoarrow provides that conversion.

library(DBI)
invisible(loadNamespace("nanoarrow"))

totals <- spark_sql(con, "
  SELECT id % 7 AS weekday, count(*) AS orders, sum(id % 100) / 100 AS total
  FROM range(1000000)
  GROUP BY id % 7
")

local <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(
  local, "spark_totals",
  arrow::as_record_batch_reader(spark_fetch(totals))
)

dbWriteTable(local, "days", data.frame(
  weekday = 0:6,
  name = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
))

dbGetQuery(local, "
  SELECT d.name, t.orders, t.total
  FROM spark_totals t JOIN days d USING (weekday)
  ORDER BY weekday
")
#>   name orders    total
#> 1  Mon 142858 70714.71
#> 2  Tue 142857 70714.29
#> 3  Wed 142857 70713.86
#> 4  Thu 142857 70714.43
#> 5  Fri 142857 70714.00
#> 6  Sat 142857 70714.57
#> 7  Sun 142857 70714.14
dbDisconnect(local, shutdown = TRUE)

The batches arrive in R as Arrow bytes, and DuckDB reads them from there; they are never converted to R vectors. They are on the R heap as bytes for as long as the stream lives, though: decoding each batch as it arrives is planned for a later version.

spark_disconnect(con)
